Female Striped gobies reach a maximum total length of 5.8 centimeters [Li = 5.8 centimeters], a value that represents the asymptotic size achieved by the largest individuals in wild populations. This species exhibits a modest body plan typical of many cryptobenthic gobiids inhabiting rocky littoral zones of the Mediterranean, where crevice-dwelling and a small adult size confer advantages in predator avoidance. The length-weight relationship derived from field-captured specimens indicates that a female of this ultimate length attains a corresponding wet weight of 1.7 grams [Wwi = 1.7 grams], a mass that reflects the compact, fusiform body shape characteristic of the genus Gobius. This ultimate body mass places the Striped goby among the smaller members of its family, with congeners such as the black goby (Gobius niger) reaching considerably larger sizes. Growth trajectories in this species are likely constrained by the limited availability of high-quality invertebrate prey within their preferred microhabitats, resulting in a relatively modest maximum size compared to other demersal fishes in the same coastal assemblage. Field surveys also suggest that local variation in food abundance and water temperature can affect the ultimate size attained, with individuals from more productive sites occasionally reaching slightly larger dimensions.

Sexual maturation in Gobius vittatus is initiated once individuals cross a size threshold defined by a total length at puberty of 3.28 centimeters [Lp = 3.28 centimeters]. At this developmental milestone, the corresponding body mass reaches 0.29 grams [Wwp = 0.29 grams], a value that marks the point at which energy is directed toward gonad development rather than continuing exclusively toward body growth. Field surveys and histological examinations of dissected gonads have confirmed that the onset of gametogenesis in both sexes coincides closely with this length, which represents approximately fifty-seven percent of the ultimate female length. The transition from a pre-reproductive juvenile to a reproductively competent adult is therefore tightly coupled to size rather than to chronological age alone, a pattern common among teleosts inhabiting seasonally variable environments where growth rates fluctuate with temperature and food availability. Individuals maturing at this size are likely to experience a trade-off between early reproduction and future fecundity, as smaller females typically produce fewer oocytes per spawning event compared to larger, more experienced individuals within the population.

Embryonic development proceeds rapidly under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C], with eclosion occurring after 6.5 days [ab = 6.5 days] following egg fertilisation. The newly emerged prolarvae carry a modest yolk reserve that sustains them through the non-feeding lecithotrophic phase, during which they remain largely inactive, hovering near the substrate. At the moment of hatching, each yolk-sac larva possesses an initial body mass of approximately 0.00016 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00016 grams], a value consistent with the small egg dimensions typical of the genus—egg length of 1.5 millimeters and width of 0.45 millimeters, parameters derived from measurements on the closely related black goby. This minute birth mass reflects the limited maternal investment per offspring, a strategy that favours the production of numerous small eggs over fewer, larger ones, thereby maximising the number of dispersal units in a variable recruitment environment. Following yolk resorption, which typically concludes within a few days, the larvae begin exogenous feeding on small zooplankton, initiating a rapid growth phase that continues through the juvenile stage until the onset of sexual maturation.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the Mediterranean coastal waters inhabited by this species (18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C]), Striped gobies can persist for up to 5 years [am = up to 5 years], though longevity in natural settings may be somewhat shorter owing to predation pressure and seasonal resource fluctuations. A five-year maximum lifespan (5 years) [am = 5 years] characterises this species as a relatively short-lived iteroparous fish, a life-history strategy commonly observed among small gobiids that experience high adult mortality rates at a temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C]. Over the course of this lifespan, reproductive output is concentrated in a restricted window of activity, with reproductively active females achieving a peak spawning intensity of approximately one to three clutches per week [F_R_i = approximately one to three clutches per week]. Each clutch typically contains roughly 50 to 60 adhesive eggs [N_R_i = roughly 50 to 60 adhesive eggs], and the combination of frequent spawning events with a modest clutch size allows the production of several thousand eggs over the course of a single breeding season, thereby compensating for the high mortality experienced during the early pelagic larval phase. This combination of a moderate lifespan, early maturation, and high fecundity positions Gobius vittatus as a classic r-selected species within the Mediterranean gobiid community.

The maximum reproductive rate calculated for female Striped gobies under optimal conditions at 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C] corresponds to a daily output of approximately 8.3 eggs per female per day [Ri = approximately 8.3 eggs per female per day] when averaged over the breeding period. This figure is derived from observations of females producing clutches containing roughly 50 to 60 adhesive eggs each, with spawning events occurring at intervals of every six to seven days throughout the extended reproductive season. Over a full breeding season, this translates to an annual fecundity that can exceed eight thousand eggs per female, underscoring the substantial investment in offspring production that characterises this species. The capacity for rapid repeated spawning, combined with the relatively short time required for embryonic development at the prevailing thermal regime (6.5 days [ab = 6.5 days]), allows multiple cohorts to be produced within a single warm season, enhancing the probability that at least some progeny will encounter favourable conditions for settlement and juvenile survival at a temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C]. This reproductive strategy is well suited to the fragmented and ephemeral rocky habitats that the species occupies.
